brief.outcome: Turn the owner's 12 years of wedding photography into an online course that teaches other photographers to price and sell wedding packages, and sell 100 places in the first launch within four months, without promising anyone income results.

research.approach: Course creators who sell on the first attempt prove demand before they build the whole course. They write a one-sentence outcome, sell it to people they can reach with a real start date and price, and build one module ahead of students. They count how many of their followers are the buyer and not just fans, build a waitlist before the cart opens, and warm it up for about two weeks with a free workshop or lesson and a short email series ending in a real deadline. Before opening the cart they test checkout and a fresh-student account, and they state the refund rule. They avoid outcome promises they cannot prove, and they read results by step: waitlist, workshop attendance, sales page visits, sales and refunds.

sources.title: Course launch checklist (SchoolMaker)
sources.note: 17 steps in three phases: define the promise, validate, pick a platform, build the sales page, test payment, build the list, then launch week and review. Pitfalls: treating a poll as proof of payment, untested checkout, fake urgency, outcome promises you cannot establish. Vendor page, updated 2026-10-29.

sources.title: How to sell an online course before you build it (Kajabi)
sources.note: Write the outcome in one sentence, sell a first cohort with a start date six to eight weeks out, decide the green-light number beforehand, build one module ahead of students, refund in full if you cannot deliver. Vendor page.

steps.name: Count who in the audience is the buyer
steps.why: A list of past clients and fans of wedding photos is not a list of photographers who would buy a pricing course.

steps.name: Test demand with real photographers and a pre-sale
steps.why: A poll is not proof of payment; real money or a firm commitment is.

steps.name: Choose the offer, price, platform and launch type
steps.why: The owner must pick from costed options, with a start date and refund rule.

steps.name: Write the outline, sales page, guarantee and honest claims
steps.why: One concrete outcome and truthful proof; no outcomes that cannot be shown.

steps.name: Warm the audience with a free workshop and emails
steps.why: A two-week warm-up with a real deadline turns a list into buyers.

steps.name: Test checkout and a fresh student journey
steps.why: Failed payments, login links and support contact are launch killers.

steps.name: Open the cart, answer objections and close on a true deadline
steps.why: Launch week is where sales happen; answers must use the real offer terms.

steps.name: Read results by step and keep the learnings
steps.why: Without review the next cohort repeats the same gaps.

pitfalls.text: Assuming followers and past clients are the buyers when most are couples.
Treating positive poll answers as proof that people will pay.
Launching with an untested checkout or student access.
Fake countdown timers or promised outcomes, which break trust and the owner's rule.
Keeping money for a course never delivered; refund in full when delivery fails.

stages.name: Pin down the goal, limits and the audience question
stages.goal: Turn the owner's words into a measured goal, limits and the data we can reach. Writes BRIEF.md.

stages.name: Count who is in the audience
stages.goal: Tag the 900 list contacts and read Instagram Insights to count photographers, couples, past clients and others, and note photographer questions about pricing.

checks.name: Counts are by group with how each was made; guesses are marked
No names or email addresses are written to project files
Photographer questions about pricing are listed with where they came from

stages.name: Study comparable photographer courses
stages.goal: List what comparable courses promise, charge, how they are delivered, and what refund terms and platform fees apply.

checks.name: At least five courses with price, format and date read
Outcome claims on those pages are listed as claims, not as proof
At least three course platforms are compared on fees, checkout and student access

stages.name: Talk to photographers and record what they say
stages.goal: Plan five to eight conversations with photographers the owner knows and sort the answers by pain, willingness to pay and price named.

checks.name: Answers come from real photographers, with the count shown, and not from the AI
Each answer separates what they like from what they would pay for
Outreach drafts are for the owner to send

stages.name: Check that 100 sales is reachable
stages.goal: Work back from 100 sales through sales page visits, workshop attendance and waitlist to the number of photographers the owner can reach, using ranges, and check the list can be emailed about this offer.

checks.name: The steps from audience to 100 sales are shown with a low, middle and high rate, each labelled assumed or sourced
States plainly the size of the gap if the reachable photographers are far fewer than needed
Notes whether past clients agreed to marketing emails and what an unrelated offer risks
Ends with REACHABLE, STRETCH or NOT LIKELY and what would change it

stages.name: Find the strongest offer and the gaps
stages.goal: Test the hypotheses against the audience count, comparable courses and photographer answers. Keep competing explanations.

checks.name: Every hypothesis is SUPPORTED, REFUTED or UNKNOWN, with evidence
Demand findings state how many photographers answered; under five is marked low-confidence
Each main finding names a competing explanation

stages.name: Rank the launch routes
stages.goal: Build two or three launch routes (for example pre-sell a founding cohort with a start date, build one module then sell, or workshop-led launch) with platform, price scenarios, ad use up to $1,000, owner hours, risk, and how each is measured. State what each route can reach against 100.

checks.name: Every route has price, platform cost, ad spend, owner hours, risk and how success is measured
Each route names the green-light number for going ahead before the whole course is built
The route's expected sales are shown as a range against 100, not a promise
Each route states a refund rule and what happens if the course cannot be delivered

stages.name: Owner chooses
stages.goal: The owner picks the route, price, platform and green-light number. Ask why when a top option is passed over, and record it.

checks.name: Chosen and passed-over options and the reasons are recorded
The refund rule is agreed before anything is sold

stages.name: Write the course outline and first lessons
stages.goal: Turn the promise into a short outline of lessons, with the first module's lesson plans, exercises and recording notes sized to what the owner can record.

checks.name: The course promises one concrete skill in one sentence that does not state income or booking results
Each lesson traces to a pain photographers named
The recording plan fits the owner's time and equipment
Examples from the owner's own work are marked as the owner's experience

stages.name: Write the sales page, guarantee and checkout plan
stages.goal: Write the sales page copy, the guarantee and refund wording, the checkout steps and the plan for testing a fresh student journey.

checks.name: No sentence states or implies income, pay rise or bookings students will get
Start date, workload, access length, prerequisites and refund rule are stated
Every proof point is real and marked with its source, or left out
Any deadline is a real one the owner will keep

stages.name: Plan the free workshop
stages.goal: Write the outline of a short free live workshop that teaches one pricing idea from the course, with a fair way to introduce the offer.

checks.name: The workshop teaches something usable on its own
The offer is introduced once, with the real terms
No income promises are made

stages.optional_when: The chosen route has no workshop.

stages.name: Write the launch emails and posts
stages.goal: Write the two-week warm-up emails, the cart-open and closing emails and matching Instagram posts, in the owner's voice, with a real deadline.

checks.name: Past clients get a different, lighter message than photographers
Every email states the offer terms and refund rule the same way as the sales page
No income promises or invented proof
All messages are drafts for the owner to send

stages.name: Run the launch one approved action at a time
stages.goal: Register the expected result of each step, then with the owner's approval set up the platform and checkout, test a purchase and a fresh student, publish the page, run the workshop, send the emails and open and close the cart.

checks.name: Each step has its expected result written down before it goes live
A test purchase, a failed payment and a fresh student login are tested before the cart opens
The page, checkout and emails show the same price, dates and refund rule
What is live matches what the owner approved
Any ad spend is approved and capped at $1,000

stages.name: Read the launch by step
stages.goal: Read waitlist, workshop attendance, page visits, sales, refunds and spend against 100 sales and the guardrails.

checks.name: Each step from waitlist to sale is shown with its conversion and the number behind it
Refunds, complaints and ad spend are checked against the limits
No conclusion about price or message from fewer sales or visits than the plan set; otherwise INCONCLUSIVE
The gap to 100 is shown

stages.name: Keep what we learned
stages.goal: Close the launch, record what worked and what did not, propose rules with their scope, and plan the next cohort or an evergreen version.

checks.name: Every step and test is closed with a verdict
Each rule says if it holds for this launch, this course or all courses

hypotheses.statement: Most of the 18,000 followers and 900 contacts are couples and past clients, not photographers, so the reachable buyer audience is much smaller than it looks.
hypotheses.test: Count photographers in the tagged list, Insights data and DMs.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Photographers are a small share of each group.

hypotheses.statement: Photographers will pay for a course on pricing and selling wedding packages.
hypotheses.test: Interview answers and pre-sale or deposit sign-ups, with the green-light number set beforehand.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Enough photographers name a price and commit.
hypotheses.refute_if: Few commit or the price named is far below the plan.

hypotheses.statement: 100 sales from this audience and up to $1,000 of ads is a stretch.
hypotheses.test: Work back from 100 through visits, attendance and waitlist with low, middle and high rates.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The needed waitlist is far above the reachable photographers.
hypotheses.refute_if: The needed waitlist is within reach.

hypotheses.statement: The price that photographers accept is below what the owner expects.
hypotheses.test: Prices named in interviews and comparable course prices.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Named prices cluster below the plan.
hypotheses.refute_if: Named prices match or exceed it.

hypotheses.statement: Photographers will not buy a pricing course without proof the method works, and the owner cannot state income results.
hypotheses.test: Which proof the owner can show without results promises (method, examples, own business facts), and what comparable pages use.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Buyers ask for results the owner cannot claim.
hypotheses.refute_if: Method and teaching proof are enough.

hypotheses.statement: Sales will be lost to an untested checkout or student access path.
hypotheses.test: Test purchase, failed payment and a fresh student account before the cart opens.

measurement.window: Read the funnel daily during launch week and weekly during the warm-up; read refunds for the refund period after close.
measurement.min_volume: No verdict on a price or message from fewer than 30 page visits or five photographers' answers; the go or no-go on building the full course uses the green-light number the owner set beforehand.
measurement.stop_rule: Pause the sale if checkout or access fails, if an income claim is found in any message, or if ad spend reaches $1,000; refund in full if the course cannot be delivered.
